newsitem.title: USA: IMF panel opposes excessive currency volatility.
newsitem.headline: IMF panel opposes excessive currency volatility.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund's policymaking Interim Committee came out on Monday against excessive volatility in currency markets.
"The committee agreed that exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals and that the reemergence of large external imbalances should be avoided," a statement issued by the committee said.
The committee, in an apparent reference to the dollar's rise over the past two years, said that substantial misalignments among major currency rates have been corrected.

"Excess volatility and significant deviations (in currency rates) from fundamentals are undesirable," the committee said. In that regard, it said it recognized the importance of cooperation among nations in currency markets, as appropriate.
The message in the Interim Committee communique on currency rates echoed a statement made on Sunday by the powerful Group of Seven industrialized nations.
In its statement, the Interim Committee welcomed what it called the generally favorable outlook for the world economy, but added that policy challenges remain.

"Among the advanced economies, countries where growth has been relatively strong face the challenge of sustaining the expansion while preventing an upturn in inflation, and policies should continue to be directed towards those objectives," the IMF panel said in an apparent reference to the United States and Britain.
The committee said that prospects for continued recovery appear more favorable in Japan. It urged rigorous implementation of Japan's deregulation plans as well as appropriate budget cuts.
The economic outlook has also improved in continental Europe, but high unemployment points to the need to tackle labor market rigidities there quickly, the Interim Committee said.
It backed continued efforts by European nations to meet tough budget criteria set out for participation in European monetary union in 1999, as well as structural economic reform.

"(Both) are needed for ... the longer term prosperity of the participating countries and to ensure a successful EMU that would contribute to the stability of the international monetary system," the panel said.
The committee, however, failed to reach agreement on proposals to expand the IMF's capital and to allow it to issue more of its artificial currency, the Special Drawing Right, to member nations.
